t: Research Bite #31: Learning from Errors
q: This source is a psychological review article discussing the benefits of learning from errors, arguing against the common educational practice of emphasizing error avoidance.

Experimental evidence is presented suggesting that making mistakes followed by corrective feedback can significantly enhance learning and memory, particularly when individuals are confident in their incorrect responses.
The behavioral and neurological data reviewed here indicate that, as long as one is not amnesic, making errors can greatly facilitate new learning

Individuals who are “prevention-focused” are concerned with avoiding mistakes, and “entity theorists” (who believe intelligence is fixed) may view errors as evidence of low intelligence and avoid them.

Teachers need to handle errors sensitively and avoid gratuitous punishments (verbal or otherwise). Implementing strategies like Error Management Training (EMT), which explicitly frames errors as learning opportunities, or fostering an “incremental mindset” is necessary to buffer these potential negative effects.

American classrooms have traditionally emphasized avoiding errors, with teachers often ignoring or disregarding incorrect responses. A shift to allowing and engaging with errors requires significant changes, including in-depth discussion of the reasons behind both correct and incorrect answers, which may require different skills and more time.

The framework presented is about using errors during “initial learning and during practice and preparation” for a test that counts, not allowing errors in “situations that counts” where consequences are severe. Teachers must distinguish between practice environments and evaluative ones.

t: How Flat Should Your Organization Be
q: Fewer layers between the CEO and frontline team members have so many benefits that it is reasonable to ask why organizations need layers at all.
The problem with that vision is the nature of people and decision-making. Without the structure of hierarchy, decision-making about anything important becomes rife with conflict and disagreement.
With only two or three layers, decision-making can become too centralized, concentrating too much power in the hands of only a small set of people to control key decisions.
The best organizations figure out how to come together in whatever combination, layering, and centralization are necessary to add the greatest value to the enterprise.
Good leaders don’t deny the need for hierarchy, but neither do they create layers without a strong reason. Unnecessary layers are better for cakes than organizations.

t: Why Some People Are Clutch
q: The idea of being “clutch” refers to any person who performs exceptionally well under pressure or in high-stakes moments.
Clutch players and team members tend to have high confidence in their skills, which gives them a sense of control over unfolding situations.
Not surprisingly, clutch performers regulate their emotions in a very specific way. They channel any anxiety they feel and turn it into excitement.
They get ready for the big moments by practicing maneuvers that replicate high-pressure situations.
Clutch doesn’t reside in people. Clutch is the outcome of a highly committed performer willing to do what it takes.

t: Team Members Who See Their Role as Just a Job
q: Team members who view their work and role as a job operate very differently from those who see their current position as a stepping stone in a career.

Career-minded team members invest more emotional energy in their work, develop their skills more aggressively, engage with work and colleagues more actively, and take more pride in their accomplishments.
Good leaders promote a career orientation by engaging team members in planning for their future.

This is best done by working with them to map out the actionable steps to achieve advancement. The skills they must acquire or develop, the experiences they must realize, and the relationships they must nurture are all part of this mapping.
People who do “jobs” are generally more detached and transactional. They seldom own problems or go above and beyond to create quality outcomes.

t: When Failure Feeds the Flame
q: Educational psychology, like all sciences, depends on its ability to learn from its own missteps. Few theorists have embraced this more openly and fully than John Sweller.
CLT, he contends, has matured precisely because it failed to replicate in different situations. A worked example effect that held for algebra disappeared in geometry and physics.
This insight explains why instructional strategies like worked examples are so effective for beginners -- but may backfire for experts, who find them redundant or even constraining.
CLT also sheds light on a counterintuitive finding: conditions that induce more cognitive effort -- and even more errors -- during instruction, often produce better long-term retention.
This distinction dissolves a longstanding myth in progressive education -- that discovery is always the most 'natural' and therefore the most effective form of learning.
For educators, the implications are clear: effective teaching is not about showmanship or trend-chasing. It is about aligning instruction with the reality of how our brains work.

t: What Should I Discuss at My One-on-Ones
q: Best practice suggests that one-on-one meetings between a leader and a team member should occur weekly and be driven by the report, not the leader.

By insisting that team members drive the meeting, the discussion is more likely to become a two-way dialogue, as opposed to the one-way monologues leaders too often create when they control the meeting from the outset.
The ideal structure for a weekly one-on-one is the 10-10-10 format: 10 minutes for the direct report to share what they want to discuss, 10 minutes for the leader to provide feedback

One topic often overlooked is a discussion of talent below the direct report. Discussing who is on track or off track and what talent issues should be on the leader’s radar shouldn’t wait for talent reviews.
One-on-ones are the building blocks of alignment, accountability, and relationships. Good leaders make them the highest priority.

t: The Cost of Borrowed Thought: A Response to 'Your Brain on ChatGPT'
q: The paper's core claim is not that AI makes us stupid -- though some headlines tried to squeeze that juice -- but that it reconfigures the mental landscape.
Brain scans show lower coherence in key cognitive bands; participants struggle to recall or explain ideas they had 'written' with AI help; and subjective feelings of ownership dwindle.

Like instant credit, it feels painless in the moment. You get what you want -- an answer, an essay, a plausible-sounding synthesis -- without having to grind it out. But the cost is deferred and will need repaying.
Participants who first drafted independently and then used AI showed no such erosion in neural coherence. In fact, the combination often improved outcomes.
This is no Luddite tract: the message is not "ban the robots," but rather, "don't invite them in too early.
We tend to equate fluency with learning, speed with competence, confidence with knowledge. But the desirable difficulty literature reminds us otherwise.

t: How To Be More Consistent Next School Year
q: All it takes is a piece of paper and something to write with.
I’ve described this particular exercise before. However, it begs repeating because it’s so effective.
Finally, draw a line from each misbehavior to the rule it breaks.
If you can’t clearly and immediately draw a line from a misbehavior to a rule, then you have to add a new rule.
Second, by reviewing your drawing this summer—and thus knowing exactly what misbehavior breaks which rule—you’ll be able to enforce consequences without hesitation, uncertainty, or fear.

t: Cueing Attention in Time... AKA the Three Benefits of a Good Check for Understanding good-check-for-understanding/
q: These pieces usually focus on CFU as a tool of assessment for learning. They stress the value of CFU in helping teachers to diagnose the level of understanding at a whole class level.
This therefore illustrates the second benefit of a good CFU; providing retrieval opportunities which improve learning or prior material.
BUT... something unusual also happens. The 'test' group also do better in the final test on content from segment 3. This is odd, because both groups have an identical experience during segment 3.
In other words, the third benefit of a good CFU is that it works forwards into the future, aiding new learning which takes place after the check.
The art of teaching is needed to create the conditions in which the science of teaching can be usefully deployed.
Cueing attention, in both space and time, has the potentially to be a powerful educational lever. It's not easy though.

t: 3-Read Friday #77: Checks for Understanding, Cognitive Load Theory, and Borrowed Thought
q: Mike outlines three benefits from an easily implementable strategy: tell students they will be tested on the information you are about to present.
Paul provides a fascinating insight into the latest developments in Cognitive Load Theory and the implications for instruction.
This quote hit home for me: effective teaching is not about showmanship or trend-chasing, it is about aligning instruction with the reality of how our brains work.
I recently wrote about the perils of students cognitively outsourcing their homework to ChatGPT. David delves into this issue further.
I'm a sucker for reading about attention and checks for understanding, and this post by Mike ticks both boxes.

t: Does Size Matter When It Comes to Organizational Change
q: All organizations of size are made up of teams of teams. Even in organizations of hundreds of thousands of associates, a fairly small number of team leaders drive the enterprise.
The largest organizations in the world rely upon roughly 250 or fewer team leaders to push toward results and carry the strategy and message of the enterprise.
The first quality is team leader subscription. Are the team leaders fully bought in to the change, and are they willing to do what it takes to propel that transformation forward?
In far too many change efforts, team leaders don’t display their commitment through actions.

But when team leaders buy into the change, stay on message, model what they ask of others, and require team members to enact the practices that support the change, the likelihood and speed of success go way up.

t: Fighting the Cancer of a Recklessly Negative Attitude
q: It’s simply astonishing how quickly the lowest performers find each other. They seek each other out for validation, effectively forming a cabal of complaints and grievances.
By infecting others with their conspiracy theories and complaints, they build a wall of support around themselves, which is hard for leaders to break through.
A low-performing team member with a negative attitude is a cancer that can spread quickly and destroy the positivity of a team or culture.
If an attitude is a decision, then those who mindfully make a bad one seldom revoke it. Especially when they are failing.
If there are now two low performers with a negative attitude, the leader didn’t act fast enough.

t: Investing in a Library of Experiences
q: When it comes to talent development, three essential investments stand out for their impact: best practice, assessment, and experience.
As important as best practice and assessment are to improvement, it is experience that has the most oversized influence on professional growth and development.
Experiences, both planned and unplanned, shape how leaders view the world, themselves, and their leadership.
Like other “crucible” experiences, they force leaders to confront uncertainty and adapt in a dynamic environment.
Leaving the experiences a leader encounters up to chance is just too risky. A runway full of curated experiences provides the lift leaders need to reach the highest altitudes.

t: Research Bite #30: Students', Teachers', and Parents' Knowledge About Learning Strategies
q: This academic article investigates the knowledge and perceptions of learning strategies held by students, teachers, and parents.

Through a survey using concrete examples of twelve different strategies, the study measures participants’ ratings of each strategy’s effectiveness, familiarity, and likelihood of future use or recommendation.

The findings suggest that while individuals generally recognize the value of highly effective strategies like retrieval practice and distributed study, they also tend to overestimate the usefulness of less effective methods.
The research highlights the varying levels of familiarity across groups with certain strategies, suggesting a need for broader dissemination of educational research on effective learning techniques.

While they, students, and parents generally have accurate knowledge about the most effective learning strategies, such as retrieval practice and distributed study, there is still a critical need for broad dissemination of educational research and explicit instruction on how to effectively implement these strategies
Having accurate metacognitive knowledge is an important precursor for students to use effective learning strategies.

t: I'm Surprised
q: Leaders who express disappointment in people can unintentionally create a tsunami of doubt and insecurity.
When used to convey feedback, the expression “I’m surprised” carries a payload of disappointment powerfully but indirectly.

In each case, the expression of surprise indirectly conveys disagreement or distaste. But the power of the expression lies in the fact that it is exceedingly difficult for those on the receiving end not to inquire about why the leader was surprised.
But be careful not to use the expression after a good outcome or competent performance. In that context, “I’m surprised” is a back-handed compliment at best and an insult at worst.
Frankly, we’re surprised you haven’t considered the full power of this phrase before.

t: Challenges That Grow People Best
q: They know people grow fastest when they operate with autonomy. So they design challenges that require independent decision-making.
They have learned that to fully grow and develop, people need to feel both challenged and uncomfortable while also feeling safe.
People who experience adversity with low risk build resilience and confidence. When the risk of failure or judgment is too high, then a challenge can appear overwhelming and stressful.
By lowering the risk, leaders can ratchet up the challenge and enable people to grow and develop faster. Adversity is muted when the risk is low.
In the middle of every challenge lies the consequence of failure. The best leaders mitigate the risk.

t: You Trust Me So You Can Trust Them
q: Trust is not only the most essential building block of relationships and teams, but it is also the currency through which leaders become relationally wealthy.
They place their personal reputation on the line every time they confirm that someone they know can be trusted.
In contrast to others who are quick with a reference or endorsement, the best leaders treat their recommendation to trust a third party as a reflection of their personal integrity and character.
Unbeknownst to these leaders is the fact that promoting and endorsing others is the gold standard of relational exchange. It is the currency that builds, nurtures, and sustains relationships.
If you’re not trading in trust, you’re not deepening your relationships as much as you could. Can we trust you to think about this?

t: What Is Cognitive Load Theory?
q: Most participants never figured out the rule. They used a trial-and-error approach, and he observed that the repeated multiplication and subtraction was so mentally taxing that they never noticed the pattern.
It's a reminder of a simple rule of teaching: students learn what they think about. If I want students to learn something, I should do my best to get them thinking deeply about it.

Giving students a pre-worked example focuses their attention. Other strategies that involve students trying to solve problems as they learn a new concept risk the student losing the forest for the trees.
But once students gain knowledge, they tend to learn less from worked examples and more from solving problems themselves. In the research world this is called the expertise reversal effect.
The goal isn't to reduce cognitive load, it's to focus student thinking on the essential things I want them to learn.
The more I read about Cognitive Load Theory, the more I think it really is about that simple idea: students learn what they think about.

t: Is It Better to Read on Paper or an E-Reader?
q: New research from the University of Valencia, Spain, has synthesised research from the last two decades and has found that when it comes to text comprehension -- reading to learn -- that print reading on paper may still be bettering glossy new screens.

When learning to read, such as in primary school, a negative relationship was observed between leisure digital reading and text comprehension. However, for secondary and university age students, the relationship turned into a positive one.
What the research indicates is that reading 10 hours of print on paper may prove more likely to be retained.
With digital texts, we can scroll and click, but that can potentially disturb the careful act of reading.
We should be wary of a Luddite attitude to technology that rejects e-readers or digital textbooks, but at the same time we should select our mode of reading with care.
When it comes to younger children, we should give them lots and lots of exposure to traditional print (thereby developing 'print knowledge').

t: How to Teach Element 2 of 4: Transformations
q: Transformations have an input and an output. A prompt and a response.
For categoricals, response options are restricted, finite... For transformations, responses are potentially unrestricted, infinite.
No analogies about substituting footballers, no long-winded explanation, no need for any of it. 10-20s later and every kid in your class can substitute.
A simple sequence of three examples. Sometimes even fewer examples are possible for teaching transformations, just one or two. Rarely are more needed.
They adhere to the difference principle by showing minimal variation between examples, and then treating them differently.
They adhere to the sameness principle by showing a maximal variation and treating it the same as every other example.

t: A Master Class of Institutional Knowledge
q: Institutional knowledge is one of the key assets in any organization. Held by leaders and team members across the organization, this collective memory allows the organization to maintain standards, make informed decisions, and reinforce the enterprise culture.
With every team member departure, the organization has the potential to lose some of this institutional memory.
In addition to process maps and outlines, the use of video to capture real people discussing how they execute processes is a best practice.
Asking departing team members to teach a Master Class on what they have learned and how they have gone about their work is a positive experience for everyone.
Institutional knowledge represents the long-term health and currency of an enterprise. Good leaders never take it for granted.

t: 3-Read Friday #76: Teaching Transformations, Cognitive Load, and Paper vs E-Readers
q: I find Kris' Unstoppable Learning newsletter fascinating. In this post he introduces how to teach Transformation Atoms. Three carefully chosen examples, 20 seconds, and then lots of checking for understanding.
If you want a 5-minute summary of the key concepts in Cognitive Load Theory, then this is for you. There's even a comment on the post from Paul Kirschner as an added bonus.
It's a question I ponder both for myself and my 6-year-old. Alex synthesises the research.
Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
How to Teach Element 2 of 4: Transformations by Kris Boulton.

t: How To Teach Easy Lessons That Students Love
q: You don’t have to be cutesy or whimsical or clever. You must have a clear objective, of course.
Because you have something they can’t get anywhere else. You are a living and breathing expert in your content area.
It’s about teaching something cool your students don’t know much about. That’s it.
The secret to great lessons is in what you know and what they can’t get anywhere else.
Never try to compete with the online world. You’ll get crushed.

t: How Leaders Treat Failure and Error Differently
q: For leaders, failure is an event and a group activity. In other words, no one person fails. Failure is an outcome that many people contribute to.
Discussing failure in a group makes everyone accountable. Good leaders search less for reasons why something failed and spend more time on what to do differently in the future.
In contrast to failure, errors are mistakes, missteps, or oversights made by an individual. That makes discussing an error more effective if done privately, between the leader and the offender.
The permanent casting of failure when applied to individuals is a stigma that prevents people from learning and lowers confidence.
If failure is a group detour, errors are potholes that can be filled in. Neither is the opposite of success. Both pave the road for good fortune if addressed correctly.

t: What Do I Wish My Leader Knew About Me
q: Several years ago, elementary school teacher Kyle Schwartz wrote “I wish my teacher knew _______” on the board and asked her 3rd-grade students to complete the sentence.
The revelations altered her entire approach to how she wanted to teach.
They learned that school children will share their realities with teachers if they are given the invitation.
Knowing what team members confront in their lives away from the workplace isn’t about compromising on work quality or making excuses for people.
Start by sharing your own backstory and asking them for theirs. What you learn might change how you lead.

t: Is Psychological Safety Inconsistent With Candidness
q: The bottom line is this: When people believe they are protected from embarrassment, ridicule, and humiliation for what they say and do, they operate more openly and learn more actively.
Contrary to popular misconception, a psychologically safe environment is not always a comfortable or agreeable domain.
In fact, the most psychologically safe discussions occur when everyone feels they have the group’s permission to speak their mind, including the leaders.
Psychological safety arises from the commitment leaders and peers have to learning from each other and finding shared understanding and meaning through dialogue.
Too many leaders believe that kindness, support, and niceness create psychologically safe environments. Instead, they often get in the way of learning together.

t: Teams That Perform Acts of Community Service
q: Of the many teambuilding activities available to organizations, perhaps none is as powerful as team members performing a community service together.
Because it involves helping others and does not focus on the everyday work of the organization, team members drop any pretense and build camaraderie.
The key to such activities is to find a project everyone on the team wants to contribute to. Everyone must engage. No one can sit on the sidelines or choose not to contribute.

Consider this shortlist of activities: Vaccination drives and sponsoring health fairs, fostering animals awaiting adoption, disaster preparation, creating community gardens, revitalizing local parks, planting trees
Leaders who facilitate acts of service build teams in the process. When team members use their talents to serve the community, they lift themselves up and learn how to better collaborate.

t: Research Bite #29: "Are You on Slide 8 Yet?" -- Standardised Curricula and Teacher Professionalism
q: This extensive report examines the impact of standardized curricula on teacher professionalism in England, drawing on survey data from over 1600 teachers, interviews with 40 teachers, and analysis of policy documents and curriculum resources.

Key findings indicate that while widely used, standardized curricula, particularly those developed in-house by schools or multi-academy trusts, are associated with a reduced sense of teacher autonomy and self-efficacy.

Although initially perceived as a tool to alleviate workload, the research suggests these curricula often simply shift the workload burden from planning to adapting generic materials, leading to no overall improvement in teacher workload perception.

The report specifically addresses the publicly funded Oak National Academy, finding its usage to be low and primarily for supplementary or cover purposes rather than as a comprehensive curriculum plan, thus questioning the justification for significant public investment.

Ultimately, the document argues for a greater emphasis on teacher autonomy, professional development in curriculum design, and a more open and less politically driven debate about curriculum policy in England.
The central importance of their professional autonomy, self-efficacy, and role as curriculum makers

t: The Fear of Disappointing People Who Believe in You
q: They depend on the idea that you will represent their faith in you by engaging the world with competence and integrity.
The fear of disappointing people who believe in us shapes many of our choices. We show up prepared, practiced, and polished to reward them for that belief.
This fear of disappointing people who believe in us is one of the few fears that generally serve us well.
More importantly, it keeps us from taking shortcuts, compromising our standards, and trading on our integrity.
The fear of disappointing people can paralyze you. It’s evidence of the stock you have in what others think of you. But using that fear to motivate you is what good people do.

t: Making Everyday Excellence ‘Routine’
q: In the past I’ve spent most of my morning simply trying to get my class to a point where they can begin their day…often achieving this right before recess, after which the process starts all over again.

Katherine discussed the need for definitive routines without the grey area. Her example was brilliant: how can you quantify the concept of quiet corridors, as opposed to silent? My version of quiet is likely to be different from yours, therefore the expectations are already vague. Katherine also emphasised the need to keep routines consistent. How many goals or habits do we give 100% to on the first day, but perhaps 95% the next? What does that look like in 2 weeks? A term?

Personally, these explicit routines minimise noise and reduce opportunity for incidents that occur so often during less-structured transition times. Buy-in from school staff enables me to rest easy knowing that a teacher covering my class is keeping expectations consistent. For students, clear and high expectations support feelings of safety and calm, allowing attention to be given to what’s important – learning.

What is so powerful about a Do Now is its versatility. It can be a formative assessment, a task to activate prior knowledge or consolidate prior knowledge. The low-stakes nature of a Do Now means that everyone in my class has found success before 9am.

We open our doors at 8.50am each morning, with the day officially beginning at 9am. The old me wouldn’t have thought twice about those 10 minutes, it seemingly being such a tiny portion of the day. But if my students complete a Do Now every school day this year, that’s nearly 32 hours, over a week, of additional learning time.

t: Leading by Feelings Versus Principles
q: Their behaviors and choices reflect what they are feeling at any given moment. How they feel determines what they do or don’t do.
Almost by definition, people who lead and live by feelings are highly inconsistent.
As their feelings change, so do their behaviors and decisions. Leading and living by feelings is a rollercoaster.
The core set of principles good leaders live and lead by allows them to stick to their guns. Principles get them to the gym when they don’t have the energy.
Consider writing down the principles you want to lead and live by. Keep the list of personal rules and commitments tight enough so you can memorize them.

t: The Ground Rules of Disagreeing With Your Leader
q: Smart team members reserve strong disagreement for private conversations, eliminating the need for leaders to save face.
Opinions are not as powerful as facts. Whenever possible, make sure to back up your viewpoints with data.
If you can’t figure out a way to ask it as a question, you are more interested in making your point than being effective.
Disagreement without a solution, remedy, or path forward will be heard as a complaint. Constructive team members don’t just point out problems.
The ground rules require you to hold the leader in high regard. Disagreement in any other form is considered rebellious dissent.

t: Managing Attention in Classrooms Is a Social Justice Issue -issue/
q: As we might expect, there was a positive correlation between IQ and performance on the memory test; the higher the IQ the better the memory.
The correlation almost completely disappears. When children are forced by a task to engage more of their attentional resources to the task, IQ no longer has an effect on memory performance.
Remarkably, the effects of SES can be found in even 9-month-old infants.

Some students who appear to struggle with learning might, at least in some circumstances, see their deficits diminish, or even disappear, in environments where we can assist them in focusing their attention effectively.

If a core responsibility of education is giving every student the opportunity to learn as effectively as possible, regardless of their cognitive or environmental circumstances, then 'never assume attention; cue it' becomes less a pedagogical nuance and more a core requirement of equitable education.
Of course, cueing attention in the classroom is an utterly rudimentary and downright obvious part of teaching. That said, do we do it well enough, or systematically enough?

t: Experiences to Issues to Actions: Developing as a Reflective Mathematics Teacher ve-mathematics-teacher/
q: We believe that one way to do this is by developing as a reflective teacher, so that each year is different from the last.
In fact, the joke often goes that the best teacher experiences 20 different years in school rather than just one year repeated 20 times!

In the varied topography of professional practice, there is a high hard ground overlooking a swamp. On the high ground, manageable problems lend themselves to solution through the application of research-based theory and technique. In the swampy lowland, messy, confusing problems defy technical solution.

So, thinking about your domain of knowledge (the hard high ground) is a useful practice to develop, and one of the key ways that we learn new ideas and skills. But on its own, it may not be sufficient to make progress in your chosen field.
There are almost as many models of reflective practice as there are reflective practitioners!
Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle lists four stages to effective reflection: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation.

t: 3-Read Friday #75: Silence, Attention, and Reflective Practice
q: A short post with an important message: sometimes the best thing we can do as teachers is shut up.
Managing attention in classrooms is a social justice issue by Mike Hobbiss.
Are you looking for a deep dive into the research concerning attention, with practical implications? Then look no further!
Chris, a model leader on a maths PGCSE course, presents a useful framework for teachers of all experiences to apply as they reflect on their lessons.
Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.

t: Why Your Students Should Read Books, Not Screens
q: No, they don’t. In fact, any use of technology during independent reading time is a bad idea.
From reading fluency to better comprehension, it’s no comparison. More and more research is showing that old-fashion books are better for kids than the images blue-lighting their faces.
Your students need escape more than any generation before them.
They need healing time away from the metal, glass, and plastic and feel the natural fibers on their fingertips.
But you must have the courage to say no. You must swim against the tide, risk being called a Luddite.
Are screens better at improving reading than actual books? Do they deepen comprehension, speed up fluency, or enhance vocabulary acquisition?

t: Respect!
q: You guys are going to do what you do, work hard, get after it, pursue the mastery, and I'm going to just say, real nonchalant, the word 'Respect.'

The thing is, the little habit stuck. It became a source of light in an often trying school year, where I juggled a couple 35-student class sections, a couple really tricky general-level groups, and the ever-present journey of being a teacher.

This quote is an inspiration for us all to engage in the class and keep pushing for double-sided respect. If you aren't pushing for MAD Respect, what are you even doing? Step up your game and go for it; you won't regret doing so.
The simple fun we can have — even amidst the hardships. The ways in which words, especially repeated ones, can do things much bigger than the intent of the speaker.
But one thing you have to take, from one colleague to another, is the deep feeling I have when I think about writing to you. That feeling, in a word, is Respect.

t: On culture and toxic leadership
q: The research highlights that school culture significantly impacts teachers' and leaders' perceptions of workload. Workload isn't merely about hours worked but also its complexity and meaningfulness.

One of the big factors we have found is driving teachers out of school is toxic leadership and teachers being infantilised. They were horrified with the way they were patronised and infantilised when they qualified and began to teach.
From midnight emails telling me that data was needed at 8:30am the next morning to screaming at me like a child in their office, there wasn't really a day where I wasn't in tears.
I was close to suicide. One weekend... I realised I couldn't take it much more and when I started to think of ways I could kill myself causing the least fuss to my family, I knew I had to get out.

Toxic leadership can erode trust, stifle intellectual curiosity and fracture teams in schools. However, fostering a healthy school culture can serve as a buffer against these detrimental leadership behaviours.

t: Making Large Organizations Feel Smaller
q: As organizations and teams grow and add more people, it is easy to lose the camaraderie and personal connection between team members.
The more messages that are personally directed, as opposed to group chain communications, the more they recreate the conversations team members experience in smaller enterprises.
When team members get to ask the questions that matter to them and receive genuine and candid answers, they feel more connected to the organization and to each other.
Be sure to circle back and close the loop on what people suggested, even if it runs contrary to the eventual outcome.
When organizations feel smaller, they foster more connection, reduce anonymity, and create a strong sense of community.

t: Talent Retention in a World of Fast Movers
q: Leaders and team members no longer stay in the same seats for very long. They change jobs or roles on average every four years or so.
Either they are being asked to do too much or too little. In other words, they are either challenged beyond their comfort zone, or they aren’t challenged enough to grow.
Because high talent is attracted to and benefits from other high talent, good leaders seek out opportunities to expose, connect, and couple the most talented team members.
High-talent team members also desire feedback. They look for information that can propel them forward and fast-track their development.
They fight the expectations team members have of always moving to the next thing by giving them a great thing now.

t: Research Bite #28: Teaching to the Test
q: This research article examines the impact of “teaching to the test” (TTT), a practice focusing on test preparation, on secondary school students’ motivation in Austria.
While commonly viewed negatively, this study, using longitudinal data and Expectancy-Value Theory, found that students perceived an increase in TTT closer to graduation.

Contrary to expectations, this perceived increase was linked to positive changes in intrinsic motivation, perceived importance, and utility of the subject, suggesting TTT may not be inherently detrimental.
To the authors’ knowledge, this was the first study to directly examine the association and direct effects of (perceived) TTT on student motivation.
They suggest that, as in many areas, “the dose makes the poison” and teachers should strive to provide students with a variety of teaching methods, using TTT “in moderation”.

Teaching to the test (TTT), contrary to widespread concerns, might not have the detrimental effects on student motivation that many researchers and educators fear, and can even enhance some aspects of it when used strategically before exams
The study focused on motivation and did not investigate the effects of TTT on students’ actual achievement in the final exam.

t: Generating More Referrals
q: The highest endorsement any performer can receive is to have an audience share the competence they’ve witnessed firsthand with those who trust them.
Most customers, audiences, and patrons find it offensive when performers ask for referrals before they are ready to give them.
The second step is less obvious. The performer must refer the audience, customer, or patron before they make a request. People are more likely to give referrals to those who refer them first.
By requesting the referral in the form of a question, those on the receiving end of this query don’t find it awkward, especially if they are not yet ready to endorse and refer.
Aside from baseball, a strong ERA stands for “earn, refer, and ask.” Make sure to do the first two steps before the ask.

t: The Relentless Pursuit of a Personal Mission
q: Whereas goals are specific, measurable, and outcome-focused, a mission defines the core purpose that remains unchanging and always present.
A personal mission is a guide that clarifies what matters most. It provides a direction and focus that serves as a north star.
Having a personal mission helps to ensure that long-term goals don’t compete or contradict each other. It keeps a leader’s actions and ambitions integrated and authentic.
Just the act of crafting such a statement usually has a profound effect on leaders.
Once one exists, you become a missionary to your purpose. That means you are in the stubborn pursuit of fulfilling your mission every day.

t: What Leaders Should Never Pay For
q: Chief among them is compensating people for being good citizens in the organization or team.
When leaders compensate people for being helpful and collaborative, they rob them of the intrinsic motivation to cooperate with their colleagues.
Leaders who mistakenly create formalized reward systems to promote collaboration actually get less of it over time.
Once team members believe they should be compensated for supporting and collaborating with others, leaders are stuck without any other appeal to action except more money.
Compensating for collaboration creates a sinkhole of expectation and destroys team morale over the long term.

t: Retrieval Strength and Storage Strength
q: Retrieval strength refers to how easily an idea can be recalled. Storage strength refers to how durable a memory is for the long term.
High retrieval strength can fool us into thinking we have learned things that actually have low storage strength.
Repeated exposure increases retrieval strength quickly. That might seem like learning because the idea becomes easy to recall, but that learning will also fade quickly.
Storage strength increases most when retrieval strength is relatively low.
Recalling an idea when it's not fresh in your mind requires more effort, and that additional effort boosts storage strength.
First, spaced retrieval is more effective for learning than blocked retrieval.

t: I/We/You: Use with Caution
q: 'To me, I/We/You is a powerful way to conceptualise teaching specific things. It is NOT a powerful way to structure lessons. It's a cycle. And you could have multiple cycles in any given 55 minute lesson.'
Worryingly, teachers have anecdotally shared with us that they have been told to be 'on' the 'you do' phase of the lesson at a certain time, checked by observers.
It's our aim here therefore, to remind leaders to be vigilant, and forewarn that 'I/We/You' is vulnerable to lethal mutation.
Having a prescriptive lesson structure of I/We/You prevents the teacher from exercising their professional expertise to adapt the teaching in light of student feedback.
Generic, top-down strategies quite often ignore the beautiful nuances of individual subjects and lead to a 'one-size-fits-all' approach.
However, as a longer term teaching and learning strategy, it will straightjacket teacher agency to be adaptive and deploy different aspects of their toolkit when appropriate to.

q: If you consider multiplication from early multiplication to factorising double brackets, maybe you are teaching 8 different methods of multiplication?

This early connection, potentially as early as ages 4 or 5, is crucial. Students can see the different shapes, use different items before building with multilink cubes and counting squares within rectangles.

In my previous post I mentioned how historically I stopped using 'grid method'. A key difference I see is that the rebranding of the area model means that this is not simply a method for students to arrive at the correct answer; it has a deeper, connected layer.

By highlighting the diagonals within the area model grouping the place value. This understanding could then provide a natural bridge to an efficient methods like lattice multiplication, offering a strong conceptual foundation rather than a rote procedure.

t: Your 2024-25 Smart Classroom Management Report Card port-card/
q: The purpose is to assess the extent you were able to follow the principles of Smart Classroom Management.
Because it provides a clear picture of where you need to improve.
If you wish, you can add up your final numbers to earn an SCM belt rank.
However, I added the rank of red belt because it represents a jump in performance to a level of control and virtuosity that can feel as if you’re conducting the New York Philharmonic.
In other words, whatever classroom management excellence you can imagine, you’re able to make happen right in front of you.
The key is to start strong from the very first day of school.

t: Any Thoughtful, Informed Response to AI = Better Than a Mindless One
q: A one-week experiment during my writing bootcamp in which I used Claude to score and give feedback on three sets of student essays (I know, it sounds crazy).
But here is where I basically landed: at this point in the journey, I can respect any teacher or school response to AI so long as it is thoughtful.
Knowledgable about the state of the technology today, how it works, what it's capable of, what its drawbacks are. Knowledgable about how learning (growth toward mastery) and motivation work.
That said, wherever you fall on the spectrum — zero-AI, mixed-AI, all-AI — I think your students will be better off for having you as a teacher in the years to come.

It's about thoughtful engagement with not just the technology but also its ramifications for learning, motivation, and long-term flourishing. The more people like this we can get in front of our students in the years to come, the better.

t: Research Bite #27: Education and Intelligence: Pity the Poor Teacher
q: The author contends that student characteristics, particularly general cognitive ability or intelligence, account for the vast majority of variance in educational outcomes, far outweighing the impact of teachers or schools.

Research spanning decades, including the Coleman Report and twin studies, supports this claim, indicating that school and teacher-related factors contribute only a small percentage to overall achievement.
The source suggests that teachers account for only 1% to 7% of the total variance in academic achievement at every level of education.
As much as 90% of the variance in educational outcomes is associated with students, and a substantial portion of this (50% to 80%) is due to differences in intelligence.

The predicted correlation between student achievement and mean student ability could be as high as 0.95, while the correlation between teacher quality and average student gain is predicted to never exceed 0.32.
Educational gain will be best predicted by student abilities (up to r = 0.95) and much less by teachers’ skill (up to r = 0.32).
It is argued that blaming teachers for all the problems of the educational system is inappropriate.

t: Helping Reticent Team Members Find the Courage to Speak Up
q: Finding the courage to advocate, contribute, or opine on an issue or in a given situation is not always easy. People must have a good reason to expose their candid views to others.
Good leaders remind those who lack the courage to share their candid views of the many good reasons they have for speaking up.
Reticent colleagues often haven’t thought through the many reasons they should speak up.
They encourage others to think about the consequences of remaining silent.
Good leaders are not only conductors, orchestrators, educators, and directors. They are also reminders.
